hints: Focus on what effervescence tells you when any acid is added to a carbonate mixture.
Notice that solid Y must be insoluble in water, so check the solubilities of chlorides versus sulfates.
Compare calcium sulfate and magnesium sulfate for solubility to see which one can appear as a white solid.
walkthrough:
**Interpret the effervescence**

Both magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate react with acids to release carbon dioxide gas. That explains the fizzing.

$$\text{MCO}_3 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check if a solid can form with hydrochloric acid**

All common chlorides are soluble in water. Both $\text{CaCl}_2$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$ would stay dissolved, so no white solid Y would be seen.

**Check what forms with sulfuric acid**

Sulfates show a key difference. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, but calcium sulfate is sparingly soluble and forms a white precipitate.

$$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4(s) + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Conclude the identities**

Only sulfuric acid can give both effervescence and an insoluble white solid, and that solid must be calcium sulfate.

options.A: Hydrochloric acid does give effervescence with carbonates, but calcium chloride is very soluble in water. It would remain in solution, not form a white solid Y.
options.B: Hydrochloric acid does give effervescence, but magnesium chloride is also very soluble. No precipitate would form, so this cannot explain the observed white solid.
options.C: Sulfuric acid reacts with both carbonates to release $\text{CO}_2$, giving effervescence. The calcium ions then form sparingly soluble white $\text{CaSO}_4$, which appears as solid Y, while magnesium sulfate stays in solution.
options.D: Sulfuric acid is the correct type of reagent, but magnesium sulfate is soluble in water. It would not precipitate as a white solid, so Y cannot be magnesium sulfate.
